speaker: Mike Krieger
title: Anthropic's CPO on what comes next | Mike Krieger
question: In software product development, what actually changes operationally when AI writes most of the code?
guest: The role of engineering has changed a lot, though the suite of people producing a product has not yet. One of the biggest shifts is prototyping happening much earlier, where PMs or designers use AI to put together a functional demo to make an idea tangible. Still, knowing what to ask the AI and how to structure a change between the back end and front end remains a difficult, specialized engineering skill. Meanwhile, we rapidly became bottlenecked on other things. Our merge queue—getting in line for a change to be accepted and deployed to production—had to be completely re-architected because so much more code and so many more pull requests were being submitted. Using critical path theory, you find all these new bottlenecks. There is an upstream bottleneck around decision-making, alignment, and providing minimum viable strategy so people can explore. Once building happens, coordination bottlenecks emerge so teams do not step on each other's toes. And downstream, when work is complete, you hit bottlenecks around air traffic control for landing changes and launch strategy.

points.core: Non-engineers build functional prototypes earlier to make product ideas tangible.
points.note: Accept: PMs or designers using AI to build working demos or prototypes earlier in the development cycle. Do not credit: generic claims that prototyping gets faster without noting the role shift to non-engineers.

points.core: Structuring cross-stack architectural changes still requires specialized human engineering judgment.
points.note: Accept: engineers remaining essential for problem decomposition, prompting strategy, or structuring backend-to-frontend changes. Do not credit: vague statements that humans are still needed in the loop.

points.core: Surging pull-request volume rapidly overwhelms downstream merge queues before deployment.
points.note: Accept: merge queues, CI/CD pipelines, code review throughput, or release coordination breaking under much higher PR volume. Do not credit: generic claims that shipping software is still hard.

points.core: Upstream decision-making alignment replaces raw coding speed as a primary constraint.
points.note: Accept: deciding what to build, setting minimum viable strategy, or aligning teams becoming the dominant upstream bottleneck. Do not credit: generic advice that product strategy is important.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
When AI writes most of the code, the bottleneck moves from producing code to deciding what to build and confirming that what was built is correct. Writing becomes cheap; specification, review, and verification become the scarce work.

Engineers spend less time typing and more time defining intent precisely, breaking work into pieces an agent can handle, and reviewing output. Because code volume rises faster than human reading capacity, review becomes the choke point, so teams lean harder on automated tests, type checks, CI gates, staged rollouts, and observability rather than line-by-line inspection.

Planning changes too. Prototypes are cheap, so teams build several options and discard most, and the build-versus-discuss balance tilts toward building. Product, design, and engineering roles blur, since non-engineers can ship working changes.

New costs appear: codebases grow faster than anyone's understanding of them, plausible-looking defects and security issues slip through, and juniors get fewer chances to build judgment. Accountability stays human, so ownership, architecture decisions, and documentation that agents can read matter more than before.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
When AI writes most of the code, the core bottleneck in software development shifts from authoring implementation to upstream specification and downstream verification. Day to day, engineers spend far less time writing syntax and far more time defining precise constraints, maintaining clean architectural boundaries, and auditing large volumes of generated diffs. Because code output easily outpaces human review capacity, teams must invest heavily in automated harnesses—fast CI, deterministic tests, static analysis, and ephemeral preview environments—so agents can self-verify before a human ever inspects a change.

Product discovery and team topology shift alongside the workflow. Instead of debating static mocks and effort estimates, product, design, and engineering spin up disposable working prototypes directly, collapsing traditional handoffs. Meanwhile, operational risk migrates toward subtle architectural drift, security regressions, and debugging production incidents in unfamiliar generated code. With implementation cheap, smaller teams own much broader surface areas, and delivery speed is governed less by coding headcount than by product judgment, modular system design, strong observability, and review throughput.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
When AI writes most of the code, the bottleneck moves from typing code to specifying what to build and checking what got built. Writing code gets cheap. Review, testing and integration become the limiting steps, so teams put more effort into automated test suites, CI gates, type systems and evaluation harnesses that can catch mistakes in output nobody wrote by hand.

The work engineers do changes with it. They spend more time decomposing problems, writing clear specs and context documents, supervising agents and reading diffs critically, and less time writing implementations. Pull requests get bigger and more frequent, and review fatigue becomes a real risk. Ownership and accountability need explicit rules, because someone still has to understand and answer for code they didn't write.

Prototyping gets so cheap that teams build several versions and compare them instead of arguing in advance. That pushes product management toward faster experimentation and harder prioritization. The risk profile changes too: subtle bugs, security holes, dependency sprawl and codebases that drift because generated code is locally plausible but architecturally inconsistent. So architecture standards, observability and staged rollouts become more important.

Team shape follows: fewer pure implementers, more senior judgment per person, and new tasks like managing prompts, context and agent tooling.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
When AI writes most of the code, the primary operational bottleneck shifts away from implementation speed and toward specification, verification, and integration. Because generating code becomes cheap and fast, pull request volume rises sharply, quickly overwhelming traditional human line-by-line code review. Teams respond by investing much more heavily in automated test suites, strict CI/CD gates, static analysis, type safety, and production observability so quality is enforced systematically rather than manually.

Day-to-day engineering work also rebalances. Developers spend less time writing boilerplate or syntax and more time decomposing problems, defining clear acceptance criteria, curating architectural boundaries, and auditing AI-generated changes for subtle edge cases, security flaws, or silent technical debt. Upstream, cheap prototyping blurs the line between design and engineering, letting product teams test working software instead of static mockups. Ultimately, throughput stops being constrained by how fast a team can type and becomes constrained by how clearly it can decide what to build and prove that it works safely in production.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
When AI writes most of the code, the cost of producing a first draft drops. Teams can try more ideas and get working prototypes in front of users sooner. The bottleneck often moves to deciding what to build, verifying that it works, and getting it safely into production.

Day to day, engineers spend more time turning product intent into clear acceptance criteria, giving AI the right codebase context, and reviewing changes for behavior, security, and maintainability. Small changes, automated tests, and production monitoring matter more because a team can generate changes faster than it can scrutinize them. Engineers still own what ships and debug it when it breaks.

The practical test is whether the team delivers useful changes faster without increasing defects, rework, or review queues. If it can write twice as much code but still takes just as long to ship a reliable feature, it has accelerated one step of the process.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
When AI writes most of the code, a developer can produce a candidate change in minutes. The team still has to decide whether it solves the right problem and is safe to ship. That shifts the bottleneck toward specifying behavior, reviewing changes, and verifying how they work in the product.

Day to day, developers give the AI context and acceptance criteria, inspect its changes, and test assumptions it may have missed. For example, an AI can quickly implement a refund flow. Someone still has to decide what should happen if a customer clicks twice and verify that the payment system issues only one refund.

If code arrives faster than people can review it, the review queue grows. Small changes, automated checks, and production monitoring help teams turn faster coding into faster releases. The practical measures are time from idea to a verified release, whether customers get the intended result, and how often changes cause failures.
